What Makes a Generalist Robot Policy?

A study of how model choice, simulation, multi-task learning, and egocentric human demonstrations contribute to more generalist robot policies in a low-cost bimanual setup.

Tristan Meynier · Independent Researcher, Switzerland · 2026

Paper source Code & data
00 / Abstract

Research question and scope

Recent advances in AI and robotics have steadily broadened the scope of learned robot policies. The progression begins with single-task behavior-cloning policies such as ACT, extends through simulation data that increases experience beyond physical demonstrations, and now includes pretrained vision-language-action models that inherit large-scale visual and language representations. Multi-task, multi-embodiment, and egocentric human datasets create further opportunities to share skills across tasks and bodies.

Together, these developments aim to improve robustness and generality, but their individual contributions are difficult to separate. This study measures the incremental benefit—and limitations—of each ingredient on a low-cost 12-DoF bimanual robot. Through matched ablations, we compare ACT and π0.5, real-only and real-plus-simulation training, single-task specialists and a shared seven-task policy, and π0.5 with and without aligned egocentric RGB-D human demonstrations.

02 / Task suite

The tasks

Seven tasks in one workspace span grasping, visual conditioning, articulated and precision manipulation, bimanual coordination, and long-horizon sequencing. The suite tests skill transfer across tasks.

Foundational

03 / Data

The data

1 · How is simulation added?

The training budget stays fixed. The real-only run fills the simulation slots by sampling the same real demonstrations again. The real + simulation run uses simulated episodes in those slots instead. So the comparison changes the source of experience, not the number of training updates.

2 · Human video has no robot action—what do we do?

RGB-D hand tracking turns each hand's motion into relative 6-DoF end-effector “pseudo-actions,” matching π0.5's Cartesian action format. Ego batches replace part of the simulation mix, keeping real-data sampling and the total training budget unchanged. This is used for π0.5, not ACT.

04 / Results

Our results

Task success is measured from closed-loop rollouts. Longer tasks also use partial-success metrics. Generalization is evaluated on a previously unseen task. Recovery is tested through object displacement.

06 / Conclusion

Conclusion

Within this setup, the ablations show that generalization benefits from diversity across data sources, embodiments, and tasks:

  • Real-robot demonstrations: Slow and costly to collect, but essential for grounding perception and control in the robot's real dynamics.
  • Simulation: Cheap to scale and randomize, adding varied states and perturbations that improve robustness without additional physical trials.
  • Vision-language pretraining: Reuses internet-scale image–text data, giving the policy broad visual and semantic context about objects, scenes, and instructions.
  • Egocentric human video: Easier to collect than robot trajectories and adds task experience from another embodiment, supporting human-to-robot transfer.
  • Multi-task demonstrations: Require examples for each task, but let a shared policy refine common representations and transfer useful skills across tasks.

Together, these ingredients help the policy build a richer internal representation of the world—similar to how broad, varied training supports transfer in large language models.
